claim: Bundles of cytoskeletal filaments and molecular motors generate motion in living cells.
source: Bundles of cytoskeletal filaments and molecular motors generate motion in living cells, and have internal structures ranging from very organized to apparently disordered.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in cell biology supported by general scientific knowledge.

claim: Cytoskeletal bundles have internal structures ranging from very organized to apparently disordered.
source: Bundles of cytoskeletal filaments and molecular motors generate motion in living cells, and have internal structures ranging from very organized to apparently disordered.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to experimental observations in the introduction.

claim: Existing models predominantly predict that disordered cytoskeletal structures are contractile.
source: The mechanisms powering the disordered structures are debated, and existing models predominantly predict that they are contractile.
evidence: This is supported by references to theoretical literature discussed in the introduction.

claim: Self-organization in cytoskeletal bundles results from the interplay between filament assembly/disassembly, motor attachment-detachment dynamics, and crosslink attachment-detachment dynamics.
source: We reexamine this prediction through a theoretical treatment of the interplay between three well-characterized internal dynamical processes in cytoskeletal bundles: filament assembly and disassembly, the attachement-detachment dynamics of motors and that of crosslinking proteins.
evidence: This is the central theoretical framework developed in the manuscript.

claim: Self-organization in cytoskeletal bundles allows for reversals of the filaments' apparent velocities.
source: The resulting self-organization is easily understood in terms of motor and crosslink localization, and allows for an extensive control of the active bundle mechanics, including reversals of the filaments' apparent velocities and the possibility of generating extension instead of contraction.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction derived from the model presented in the manuscript.

claim: Self-organization in cytoskeletal bundles allows for the possibility of generating extension instead of contraction.
source: The resulting self-organization is easily understood in terms of motor and crosslink localization, and allows for an extensive control of the active bundle mechanics, including reversals of the filaments' apparent velocities and the possibility of generating extension instead of contraction.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction derived from the model and supported by calculations.

claim: The reversal from contraction to extension mirrors some recent experimental observations.
source: This reversal mirrors some recent experimental observations, and provides a robust criterion to experimentally elucidate the underpinnings of both actomyosin activity and the dynamics of microtubule/motor assemblies in vitro as well as in diverse intracellular structures ranging from contractile bundles to the mitotic spindle.
evidence: This is supported by references to experimental work mentioned in the discussion.

claim: Many cellular functions, from motility to cell division, are driven by molecular motors exerting forces on actin filaments or microtubules held together by crosslinking proteins.
source: Many cellular functions, from motility to cell division, are driven by molecular motors exerting forces on actin filaments or microtubules held together by crosslinking proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge in cell biology.

claim: Many cytoskeletal structures do not display any apparent spatial organization of their components.
source: This wide variety of processes is powered by an equally wide range of structures, many of which do not display any apparent spatial organization of their components (Verkhovsky et al., 1995; Cramer et al., 1997; Medalia et al., 2002; Kamasaki et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple experimental citations.

claim: Actomyosin structures are overwhelmingly observed to contract.
source: While actomyosin structures are overwhelmingly observed to contract (Murrell et al., 2015), the mechanisms underlying this contraction are unclear, as individual motors can in principle elicit extension just as easily as contraction (Figure 1a–b; Hatano, 1994; Sekimoto and Nakazawa, 1998; Lenz et al., 2012a; Mendes Pinto et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by experimental citations.

claim: The mechanisms underlying actomyosin contraction are unclear.
source: While actomyosin structures are overwhelmingly observed to contract (Murrell et al., 2015), the mechanisms underlying this contraction are unclear, as individual motors can in principle elicit extension just as easily as contraction (Figure 1a–b; Hatano, 1994; Sekimoto and Nakazawa, 1998; Lenz et al., 2012a; Mendes Pinto et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by theoretical citations showing that motors could produce either contraction or extension.

claim: Individual motors can in principle elicit extension just as easily as contraction.
source: While actomyosin structures are overwhelmingly observed to contract (Murrell et al., 2015), the mechanisms underlying this contraction are unclear, as individual motors can in principle elicit extension just as easily as contraction (Figure 1a–b; Hatano, 1994; Sekimoto and Nakazawa, 1998; Lenz et al., 2012a; Mendes Pinto et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by theoretical work and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: One mechanism for symmetry breaking between contraction and extension is based on mechanical nonlinearities such as buckling of individual filaments under compression.
source: The first one is specific to actin filaments, which are very flexible, as it is based on the idea that mechanical nonlinearities, for example, the buckling of individual filaments under compression could suppress the propagation of extensile forces and thus favor contraction (Dasanayake et al., 2011; Lenz et al., 2012b; Ronceray et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical models.

claim: A second mechanism for symmetry breaking is relevant for microtubule-based systems where some motors may dwell on the ends of filaments.
source: The second mechanism is relevant for microtubule-based systems, where some (but not all) motors may dwell on the ends of the filaments, which transiently generating a type of organization similar to that found in muscle (Foster et al., 2015; Tan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental and theoretical work.

claim: A third mechanism involves spatial self-organization of motors and crosslinks along undeformable, rod-like actin filaments leading to contraction.
source: Finally, in the third type of models the spatial self-organization of the bundle's motors and crosslinks along undeformable, rod-like actin filaments leads to contraction (Kruse and Sekimoto, 2002; Zumdieck et al., 2007; Zemel and Mogilner, 2009; Oelz et al., 2015; Koenderink and Paluch, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical models.

claim: Opportunities to discriminate between different contractility models experimentally remain very limited for lack of clear theoretical predictions.
source: So far, opportunities to discriminate between these models experimentally remain very limited for lack of a clear theoretical prediction setting one apart from the others.
evidence: This is an assessment of the state of the field based on the literature review.

claim: The self-organization mechanism implies that filament-motor bundles robustly extend if taken to certain parameter regimes.
source: Here we provide such a prediction, namely that the self-organization mechanism implies that filament-motor bundles robustly extend if taken to certain parameter regimes.
evidence: This is the main theoretical prediction of the manuscript, derived from the model.

claim: The qualitative change from contraction to extension is easily detectable experimentally and is not expected in models based on mechanical nonlinearities or motor dwelling.
source: This stark qualitative change from contraction to extension is easily detectable experimentally and is not expected in models based on mechanical nonlinearities or motor dwelling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the theoretical analysis comparing different models.

claim: The prediction of extension could explain the ill-understood extension observed in some microtubule systems.
source: This prediction could also explain the ill-understood extension observed in some microtubule systems (Sanchez et al., 2012; Keber et al., 2014; Roostalu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculation connecting the theoretical prediction to experimental observations.

claim: Previous studies of contractility mechanisms only involved partial treatments of the three dynamical processes.
source: Previous studies of contractility mechanisms only involved partial treatments, whereby the time scale associated with one of these dynamics was effectively assumed to be much larger or smaller than the others.
evidence: This is an assessment of prior theoretical work based on literature review.

claim: The coupled dynamics of filament polymerization, motor dynamics, and crosslink dynamics induces a spatial organization of motors and crosslinks along the filaments.
source: We show in Sec. 'Self-organization and force distribution' that the coupled dynamics of these three elements induces a spatial organization of motors and crosslinks along the filaments.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the theoretical analysis in the manuscript.

claim: The localization of motors and crosslinks in the vicinity of filament ends leads to a switch between contraction and extension.
source: Sec. 'Velocity selection and bundle tension' then demonstrates that the resulting localization of the motors and crosslinks in the vicinity of the filament ends leads to a switch between contraction and extension, as schematized in Figure 1c.
evidence: This is demonstrated through theoretical calculations and illustrated in Figure 1c.

claim: Extension arises when the motor run-length and unbinding rate are relatively large compared to the filament length and the crosslink unbinding rate.
source: In Sec. 'Qualitative predictions' , we discuss the qualitative physics underlying this switch and its experimental relevance, and show that extension arises when the motor run-length and unbinding rate are relatively large compared to the filament length and the crosslink unbinding rate, respectively.
evidence: This is derived from the theoretical analysis of the model.

claim: Self-organization dominates in tightly connected actomyosin bundles where filament buckling is hampered.
source: We find that self-organization dominates in tightly connected actomyosin bundles, where filament buckling is hampered, and that it outcompetes dwelling in microtubule systems where the filaments are long enough for end-dwelling to be a rare occurrence.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the quantitative comparison of different mechanisms.

claim: Self-organization outcompetes dwelling in microtubule systems where filaments are long enough for end-dwelling to be a rare occurrence.
source: We find that self-organization dominates in tightly connected actomyosin bundles, where filament buckling is hampered, and that it outcompetes dwelling in microtubule systems where the filaments are long enough for end-dwelling to be a rare occurrence.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the quantitative comparison of different mechanisms.

claim: The filaments in the model are rigid, ruling out contraction arising from mechanical nonlinearities.
source: The filaments are rigid, ruling out contraction arising from mechanical nonlinearities (Lenz et al., 2012a).
evidence: This is an explicit assumption of the model.

claim: The motor velocity does not depend on its position on the filament, ruling out contraction arising from end-dwelling.
source: The motor velocity does not depend on its position on the filament, ruling out contraction arising from end-dwelling (Liverpool and Marchetti, 2005).
evidence: This is an explicit assumption of the model.

claim: The insights gained from the simple treadmilling dynamics are applicable to microtubules despite their somewhat different mechanisms.
source: While the dynamics of microtubules proceeds through somewhat different mechanisms, the insights gained from this simple, analytically tractable dynamics are also applicable there, as further described in the Discussion.
evidence: This is a claim about the generalizability of the model, justified in the discussion.

claim: Viscous drag is neglected in the model.
source: Finally we neglect viscous drag, as further argued in the Discussion.
evidence: This is an explicit assumption of the model, justified later.

claim: Similar nonuniform motor distributions have previously been studied to explain the length-dependence of microtubule depolymerization rates.
source: Similar nonuniform motor distributions have previously been studied to explain the length-dependence of microtubule depolymerization rates (Varga et al., 2006; Reese et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The crosslink depletion results from the finite time required to decorate newly polymerized filament sections with crosslinks.
source: The crosslink depletion results from the finite time required to decorate newly polymerized filament sections with crosslinks, while the motor depletion arises from the time required to dress a newly created filament overlap with motors.
evidence: This is an explanation of the physical mechanism behind the depletion.

claim: The motor depletion arises from the time required to dress a newly created filament overlap with motors.
source: The crosslink depletion results from the finite time required to decorate newly polymerized filament sections with crosslinks, while the motor depletion arises from the time required to dress a newly created filament overlap with motors.
evidence: This is an explanation of the physical mechanism behind the depletion.

claim: The extension mechanism reported here differs from behaviors previously modeled in the theoretical literature in both its cause and applicability.
source: The extension mechanism reported here differs from behaviors previously modeled in the theoretical literature, both in its cause and in its applicability.
evidence: This is a comparison with prior theoretical work discussed in the following paragraphs.

claim: Extension has been observed in numerical simulations but only in situations where motors were assumed to dwell at filament ends.
source: Extension has indeed been observed in numerical simulations reported in Belmonte et al. (2017), but only in situations where the motors were assumed to dwell at the filament ends.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Belmonte et al. (2017) qualitatively predicted that extension should result from an 'antenna' mechanism similar to the depletion quantitatively modeled in this work.
source: The discussion section of this reference does however qualitatively predict that extension should result from an 'antenna' mechanism similar to the depletion quantitatively modeled here.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In Kruse and Sekimoto (2002), extensile behavior stems from the interaction between parallel, not antiparallel filaments, which is at odds with experimental observations.
source: Another instance of bundle extension is reported in Kruse and Sekimoto (2002). In that model, the extensile behavior stems from the interaction between parallel, not antiparallel filaments, which is at odds with experimental observations that bundle-wide force generation in actomyosin requires antiparallel filaments (Reymann et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a comparison with prior theoretical work, supported by citations.

claim: Bundle-wide force generation in actomyosin requires antiparallel filaments.
source: In that model, the extensile behavior stems from the interaction between parallel, not antiparallel filaments, which is at odds with experimental observations that bundle-wide force generation in actomyosin requires antiparallel filaments (Reymann et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by experimental citation.

claim: In two-dimensional numerical simulations, extensile antiparallel microtubule pairs were reported due to mid-filament binding.
source: Finally, in two-dimensional numerical simulations extensile antiparallel microtubule pairs were reported due to the fact that they typically bind halfway between the two configurations of Figure 1b, implying that their subsequent dynamics predominantly involves extensile configurations (Gao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The freedom required for mid-filament binding is likely not afforded to tightly bundled filaments.
source: The freedom required for this mid-filament binding is however likely not afforded to tightly bundled filaments, although the non-uniform motor distributions discussed here could also have contributed to the extensile behavior observed in Gao et al. (2015).
evidence: This is a speculation about the applicability of prior results.

claim: The contractile vs. extensile character of actomyosin bundles is apparent from direct imaging of reconstituted assays and cells.
source: Indeed, the contractile vs. extensile character of actomyosin bundles is apparent from the direct imaging of reconstituted assays (Thoresen et al., 2011; Reymann et al., 2012) as well as cells (Mendes Pinto et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by experimental citations.

claim: The velocity-reversal transition can be monitored in experiments where single filaments are resolved.
source: The second, velocity-reversal transition, on the other hand, can be monitored in experiments where single filaments are resolved (Murrell and Gardel, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental methods.

claim: When motor velocity outpaces treadmilling, filaments will switch from apparently plus-end-directed motion to motor-induced, minus-end-directed motion.
source: As motor velocity outpaces treadmilling, such filaments will switch from an apparently plus-end-directed motion (illustrated in Figure 2a) to a motor-induced, minus-end-directed motion.
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the model.

claim: The number of myosins in individual thick filaments is regulated dynamically in smooth muscle.
source: Such changes could also be at work in smooth muscle, where the number of myosins in individual thick filaments is regulated dynamically (Seow, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental work.

claim: The magnitude of forces and velocities predicted by the model are on par with those found in vivo, for example in the cytokinetic ring of fission yeast.
source: The magnitude of the forces and velocities predicted by our model are on par with those found in vivo, for example in the cytokinetic ring of fission yeast.
evidence: This is demonstrated through quantitative comparison with experimental values in the following sentences.

claim: Other mechanisms for contractility based on sarcomere-like crosslinking of filament barbed ends have been proposed in the specific case of fission yeast.
source: Note also that other mechanisms for contractility based on sarcomere-like crosslinking of the filament barbed ends have also been proposed in the specific case of fission yeast (Thiyagarajan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The tensions generated by the self-organization mechanism exceed those resulting from mechanical nonlinearities or motor dwelling over broad ranges of parameters.
source: In this section, we show that in addition to being on par with experimentally observed forces, the tensions generated by our self-organization mechanism exceed those resulting from mechanical nonlinearities (e.g., buckling) or motor dwelling over broad ranges of parameters, suggesting that the self-organization mechanism could be a substantial contributor to bundle tension in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is demonstrated through quantitative comparison in the following subsections.

claim: It is reasonable to assume that self-organization and buckling can operate simultaneously and contribute additively to bundle tension.
source: Filaments retain their overall linear shape outside of the buckled regions, and it is thus reasonable to assume that self-organization and buckling can operate simultaneously and that they contribute additively to the bundle tension.
evidence: This is a modeling assumption justified by the physical picture.

claim: Self-organization dominates outside of the region where buckling is allowed, which represents a substantial fraction of reasonably accessible parameter regimes.
source: Self-organization trivially dominates outside of the region where buckling is allowed, which represents a substantial fraction of the reasonably accessible parameter regimes.
evidence: This is shown through the analysis presented in Figure 6.

claim: Positional self-organization of motors and crosslinks constitutes a viable mechanism for actomyosin force generation despite the possibility of buckling-induced contraction.
source: These results support the notion that positional self-organization of motors and crosslinks constitutes a viable mechanism for actomyosin force generation despite the possibility of buckling-induced contraction.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the quantitative comparison.

claim: Motor dwelling at filament ends takes place in certain types of microtubule-associated motors and could occur in some actin-myosin systems.
source: Motor dwelling at the filament ends takes place in certain types of microtubule-associated motors (Roostalu et al., 2018; Tan et al., 2018), and could occur in some actin-myosin systems (Wollrab et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by experimental citations.

claim: The self-organization mechanism will be a substantial contributor to force generation in microtubule-motor systems not only when motors do not dwell, but also in many situations where they do.
source: We thus expect that the self-organization mechanism will be a substantial contributor to force generation in microtubule-motor systems not only in the obvious cases where motors do not dwell on the filament, but also in many situations where they do.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the quantitative comparison.

claim: Many non-muscle actomyosin structures and motor-microtubule assemblies are very dynamic, with components continuously assembling and disassembling even as they exert forces.
source: In contrast with the static organization of striated muscle, many non-muscle actomyosin structures as well as motor-microtubules assemblies are very dynamic, and their components continuously assemble and disassemble even as they exert forces on their surroundings.
evidence: This is established knowledge in cell biology.

claim: The many parameters involved in numerical simulations have until now hampered systematic explorations of all possible dynamical regimes.
source: While numerical simulations are useful to investigate these systems (Oelz et al., 2015; Kim, 2015; Ennomani et al., 2016), the many parameters involved have until now hampered systematic explorations of all possible dynamical regimes.
evidence: This is an assessment of the limitations of prior numerical approaches.

claim: The analytical approach allows derivation of a complete phase diagram for self-organized motor-filament bundles.
source: By contrast, our analytical approach allows us to derive a complete phase diagram for self-organized motor-filament bundles.
evidence: This describes the contribution of the present work.

claim: The work uncovers two previously unreported, experimentally observable transitions between bundle contraction and extension, and between plus-end-directed and minus-end-directed apparent filament motion.
source: We thus uncover two previously unreported, experimentally observable transitions between bundle contraction and extension, and between plus-end-directed and minus-end-direction apparent filament motion.
evidence: This summarizes the main findings of the manuscript.

claim: These transitions could serve as experimental signatures of self-organization-driven cytoskeletal force generation.
source: These transitions could serve as experimental signatures of self-organization-driven cytoskeletal force generation.
evidence: This is a speculation about the experimental utility of the findings.

claim: The simplicity of the underlying mechanisms makes the qualitative statements very robust despite simplifying assumptions.
source: While some of our simplifying assumptions may affect the accuracy of our quantitative predictions, the simplicity of the underlying mechanisms make our qualitative statements very robust.
evidence: This is an assessment of the robustness of the theoretical predictions.

claim: Extension is predicted whenever the filament plus end polymerizes quickly enough to induce significant crosslink depletion in its vicinity, resulting in a sarcomere-like organization.
source: Indeed, we predict extension whenever the filament plus end polymerizes quickly enough to induce significant crosslink depletion in its vicinity, resulting in a sarcomere-like organization.
evidence: This summarizes the key mechanism for extension.

claim: Crosslink depletion is insensitive to whether filament disassembly occurs through depolymerization at the minus end or cofilin-induced severing.
source: This depletion is insensitive to whether filament disassembly occurs through depolymerization at the minus end or cofilin-induced severing (Theriot, 1997).
evidence: This is an argument for the robustness of the mechanism.

claim: The model is relevant for dynamical microtubules, whose minus ends are mostly static while the plus end grows slowly before quickly retracting in a catastrophe.
source: It is additionally relevant for dynamical microtubules, whose minus ends are mostly static while the plus end grows slowly before quickly retracting in a so-called 'catastrophe'.
evidence: This is an argument for the applicability of the model to microtubules.

claim: The model will accurately predict tension resulting from plus-end depletion during the microtubule growth phase, while fast catastrophes can be seen as instantaneous filament deletion events without significant effect on bundle tension.
source: Our model will thus accurately predict the tension resulting from plus-end depletion during the growth phase, while fast catastrophes can be seen as more or less instantaneous filament deletion events without significant effect on bundle tension.
evidence: This is an argument for the applicability of the model to microtubules.

claim: Depletion is present whether crosslinks detach at a constant rate or unbind increasingly quickly under increasing force.
source: Depletion is also present whether crosslinks detach at a constant rate as assumed here, or unbind increasingly quickly under increasing force (Miyata, 1996).
evidence: This is an argument for the robustness of the mechanism.

claim: Motors are depleted on average in newer filament overlaps even in the presence of density and velocity fluctuations from small motor numbers.
source: Turning to motors, we note that although small motor numbers may add significant density and velocity fluctuations to our mean-field model, motors are depleted on average in newer filament overlaps even in the presence of these fluctuations.
evidence: This is an argument for the robustness of the mechanism.

claim: A similarly reduced force could arise in bundles densely covered by motors due to a delay in fully aligning the myosin minifilament with two antiparallel actin filaments.
source: While we describe this effect as a consequence of delayed motor binding from the surrounding solution, a similarly reduced force could also arise in bundles densely covered by motors, for instance due to a delay in fully aligning the myosin minifilament with the two antiparallel actin filaments to allow all myosin heads to fully participate in filament sliding.
evidence: This is a speculation about alternative physical mechanisms.

claim: Introducing a more complicated motor force-velocity relationship would slightly complicate the velocity dependence quantitatively, but not qualitatively.
source: Finally, while we assume that motors always exert their stall force and thus acquire a velocity inversely proportional to the effective crosslink friction, introducing a more complicated motor force-velocity relationship would slightly complicate this dependence quantitatively, but not qualitatively.
evidence: This is an argument for the robustness of the qualitative predictions.

claim: The prediction of a robust extensile regime provides a stringent test to validate or invalidate the self-organized force generation model in specific experiments.
source: Our prediction of a robust extensile regime provides a stringent test to validate or invalidate the self-organized force generation model in specific experiments.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental utility of the predictions.

claim: The absence of extension in certain parameter regimes argues against self-organization mechanisms in favor of mechanical nonlinearity or motor dwelling models.
source: As such, it constitutes an important statement even for systems in which extension is not observed, as it implies that the absence of extension in certain parameter regimes argues against self-organization mechanisms in favor of mechanical nonlinearity (in actin) or motor dwelling (in microtubules) models.
evidence: This is a logical inference about how to interpret experimental observations.

claim: The discrepancy between the model prediction and Thoresen et al.'s observations tends to disqualify self-organized contraction in that setup.
source: This discrepancy tends to disqualify self-organized contraction in this setup, and retrospectively validates the proposal made in Lenz et al. (2012b) that mechanical nonlinearities and specifically filament buckling dominate this assay.
evidence: This is an inference about which mechanism dominates in specific experiments.

claim: Self-organized force generation is likely to play a role in in vivo actomyosin contractile structures where buckling is not observed and where actin treadmilling dynamics plays a crucial role.
source: Conversely, self-organized force generation is likely to play a role in a number of in vivo actomyosin contractile structures where buckling is not observed (Cramer et al., 1997; Kamasaki et al., 2007) and where actin treadmilling dynamics plays a crucial role (Mendes Pinto et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculation about the relevance of the mechanism in vivo, supported by citations.

claim: In microtubules, extension is observed consistent with the model prediction when filament polymerization/depolymerization dynamics is blocked in vitro.
source: In microtubules, extension is observed consistent with our prediction when the filament polymerization/depolymerization dynamics is blocked in vitro (Sanchez et al., 2012; Keber et al., 2014), while both extension and contraction can arise in more complex in vivo situations (Patel et al., 2005; Foster et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison between model predictions and experimental observations.

claim: Both extension and contraction have been reported in actin bundles which cannot buckle due to their large stiffness.
source: Both extension and contraction have also been reported in actin bundles, which cannot buckle due to their large stiffness (Stam et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by experimental citation.

claim: Transitions between contraction and extension could help understand several in vivo behaviors involving alternating contractions and expansions of the actomyosin cortex.
source: Beyond steady-state contraction or extension, transitions between these two states could help understand several in vivo behaviors involving alternating contractions and expansions of the actomyosin cortex, including cell area oscillations observed during Drosophila, C. elegans, and Xenopus development (Martin et al., 2009; Solon et al., 2009; Roh-Johnson et al., 2012; He et al., 2010; Kim and Davidson, 2011; Levayer and Lecuit, 2012) or propagating actomyosin contractility waves (Allard and Mogilner, 2013).
evidence: This is a speculation about the biological relevance of the findings, supported by citations.

claim: Oscillations could arise through a Hopf bifurcation involving rapid switching between contractile and extensile metastable states in the multiple-solution regime.
source: We speculate that such oscillations could arise through a Hopf bifurcation involving the rapid switching between a contractile and an extensile metastable state in the multiple-solution regime of Figure 4.
evidence: This is a speculation about a possible mechanism for oscillations.

claim: It would be interesting to see how the mechanisms described here apply to two- or three-dimensional actomyosin assemblies.
source: It would be interesting to see how the mechanisms described here apply to two- or three-dimensional actomyosin assemblies, whose richer geometry allows for additional actomyosin force generation mechanisms (Lenz, 2014).
evidence: This is a speculation about future research directions.

claim: Positional ordering of filaments within bundles is suppressed by filament diffusion and is not observed in many disordered actomyosin bundles.
source: More refined approaches could also include discussions of the onset of positional ordering of the filaments themselves within the bundle (Kruse et al., 2001; Kruse et al., 2003; Friedrich et al., 2012). While such ordering is suppressed by filament diffusion (Zemel and Mogilner, 2009) and is not observed in many disordered actomyosin bundles (Cramer et al., 1997; Kamasaki et al., 2007), its onset during the formation of stress fibers is quite dependent on actin filament dynamics, suggesting a role for the mechanisms considered here (Hu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental and theoretical work.

claim: The onset of positional ordering during stress fiber formation is quite dependent on actin filament dynamics, suggesting a role for the mechanisms considered here.
source: While such ordering is suppressed by filament diffusion (Zemel and Mogilner, 2009) and is not observed in many disordered actomyosin bundles (Cramer et al., 1997; Kamasaki et al., 2007), its onset during the formation of stress fibers is quite dependent on actin filament dynamics, suggesting a role for the mechanisms considered here (Hu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citation to experimental work.

claim: The fundamental principles for dynamical depletion of motors and crosslinks could serve as guiding principles in understanding self-organization in the cytoskeleton.
source: Finally, the fundamental principles for the dynamical depletion of motors and crosslinks described here could serve as guiding principles in our developing understanding of self-organized contractility in the cytoskeleton (Nakazawa and Sekimoto, 1996; Kruse and Jülicher, 2000; Kruse and Sekimoto, 2002; Oelz et al., 2015; Belmonte et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a statement about the broader implications of the work, supported by citations.
